h: A poor country, a lasting democracy: Nehru's gift and his one stain
dek: In ThePrint, Ashutosh Varshney writes that India's democracy survived against every theory about income, with Nehru playing a big part, but the curbs on free speech from the First Amendment are his awkward legacy.
ank: Voters in the first general election of 1952
At most, the share of those voters who could read
body: Scholars have long argued over whether a democracy survives because of its economic structure or because of politics, meaning parties, ideology and leaders. Ashutosh Varshney, a political scientist at Brown University, reminds us that the biggest test has been income: income alone explains about three quarters of where democracy survived and where dictatorship came after 1950.

India is the big exception to this rule. It became a lower-middle-income country only around 2006-07, yet apart from the 21 months of the Emergency it stayed a democracy for nearly sixty years, while in Europe, America and Japan wealth came first and the vote for all came later. The writer says the answer lies in the Congress party, an ideological commitment to democracy, and the resolve of Nehru, who made elections the only road to power.

The early years were not easy: lakhs of deaths in the violence of Partition, more than 1.5 crore refugees, more than six hundred princely states, and revolts in Telangana and Kashmir. Pakistan got its first constitution in 1956, which was scrapped two years later, and held its first national election in 1970. By then India had held four general elections.

Nehru did not gather power into his own hands. In the states, strong regional leaders like Kamaraj or Govind Ballabh Pant ran the show, and in 1956 he had to drop the idea of collective farming in the face of Chaudhary Charan Singh's arguments. The 1952 election is an example of this resolve: 17.3 crore voters, of whom at most 20 per cent could read, ten lakh election staff, and ballot boxes carried on camels and boats.

But there is a stain too. While Ambedkar was law minister, Nehru himself fought for the First Amendment to the Constitution, which made room for curbs on the freedom to speak and to organise in the name of public order. Varshney says Nehru did not use it harshly, but later rulers did, from Indira Gandhi to the present government. That is his awkward legacy.
nazar: This article is not a hymn to Nehru but an audit, and that is its strength. At a time when blaming Nehru for every failure has become an official hobby, it is worth remembering what a huge risk it was to give an unlettered, hungry country an equal right to vote, and that the risk paid off.

But the part about the stain is just as much about today. The window of 'public order' opened in 1951 is the one through which journalists, students and activists now land in jail. What a tool made by a liberal leader becomes in the hands of the next government is a lesson that applies to every constitutional amendment.
sawal: How did a country that sent ballot boxes on camels grow afraid of speech?
ref: First Amendment to the Constitution, 1951
An amendment by the Nehru government that added grounds such as 'public order' to Article 19 and widened the room for 'reasonable restrictions' on speech. It also created the Ninth Schedule.
Ashutosh Varshney
Professor of political science at Brown University. His books on Indian democracy and communal violence, such as 'Ethnic Conflict and Civic Life', are widely discussed.
photo_note: Village scene, Amrita Sher-Gil, 1938

h: Murder over parking: the khap's idea of honour comes to the city
dek: In ThePrint, Karanjeet Kaur writes that behind killings called road rage and parking disputes lies the same male honour logic that drives honour killings in villages.
body: In police briefings such deaths are called 'road rage' or a 'parking dispute', as if they were ordinary city accidents. Journalist Karanjeet Kaur says these labels hide the real issue. Indian men have begun to kill over small 'insults', and the logic behind it is no different from honour killing: revenge through violence for a humiliation suffered in public.

She lists several recent cases. In Bengaluru in October, the scooter of Darshan, a 24-year-old delivery worker, touched a car's mirror. He apologised and moved on, but the car driver chased him for about two kilometres and rammed him. On a Mumbai local train, a young man was stabbed in a quarrel over closing the compartment door.

The most horrifying case is from Faridabad. Paramjeet Dhankhar, 42, who works in Singapore, had come home for Diwali. He had an old quarrel with a neighbour over dog dirt, parking and a broken gate. It is alleged that the same day, at the police post, Dhankhar's friends had humiliated the neighbour. In the evening the neighbour called him over to talk, and 9 of 15 bullets hit him.

The writer links this to the villages of Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, where the khap ties family honour to the choices women make. In the city, honour has attached itself to new property: the car, the parking spot, and the respect a man thinks he is owed. Every car owner has become his own khap.

The same logic works against women. In Gurugram in September, four men chased Shivani Chauhan, a 27-year-old biker, abused her, and when she ignored them, rammed her bike. A special investigation team found it was deliberate. According to the writer, her only 'crime' was that she paid no heed to the men's attention.
nazar: This article catches something important: changing the words for violence does not change its roots. By calling it 'road rage' we make it a traffic problem, when it is about masculinity, status and easy access to guns. The police are in question too, since the threat was made openly and still a life could not be saved.
sawal: How did a brushed car mirror become worth more than a life?
ref: Khap panchayat
Traditional caste and clan based councils of Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, notorious for imposing marriage rules and for cases of honour killing.
photo_note: Representative image

h: Bunker Roy's legacy: not degrees, but the habit of learning
dek: In The Wire, Dunu Roy writes that the real gift of Barefoot College's founder was not institutions but a way of testing himself, bearing hardship and learning with a laugh, which made the ordinary extraordinary.
body: Bunker Roy, founder of Barefoot College, has died at 81. Colleagues say his legacy will live on, but Dunu Roy of the Hazards Centre in Delhi asks what that legacy really is: the institutions he built, the people he inspired, his faith in the ordinary person, or the process that shaped such a remarkable man.

Bunker Roy was no star at studies but did well at sports, and he came from a rich, elite home where people become doctors, teachers or diplomats. During famine relief work in Bihar and then in Palamu, he understood that simply handing out food and water was no solution. The writer says admitting that he did not fit into what he was seeing knocked out his pride and led him to development work.

After a degree in English literature, he taught himself. The word 'Research' in the name of the Social Work and Research Centre was a sign of this urge to learn. Concrete questions came up: repairing wells, hand pumps, literacy, debt and markets. This institution later became Barefoot College, inspired by China's 'barefoot doctor' manual, and its solar power work drew the world's attention.

Equality was the backbone of his work. In 1983 he filed a petition in the Supreme Court for minimum wages for relief workers and equal pay for women and men, and pushed for a famine to be declared in Rajasthan. Salaries at the institution were capped at the World Bank poverty line. He saw organising people for their rights as part of democracy, but chose to support it rather than lead it. The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan grew from this ground.
The writer also remembers his playful nature. In his view, self-examination, patience, bonds with people and questioning with a laugh are the heart of that legacy.
nazar: At a time when development is measured in the language of big budgets, apps and experts, Bunker Roy's work reminds us that a village woman can also become a solar engineer if someone trusts her. Dunu Roy's honest tribute does not make him a saint, and that is its virtue.

The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan, which fought for the right to information, came from this ground. In an age when the government itself shies away from transparency, the accountability Bunker Roy demanded of voluntary organisations matters even more.
sawal: How many organisations today still tie their salaries to the poverty line?
ref: Barefoot College
An institution set up by Bunker Roy in Tilonia, Rajasthan, known for teaching rural people without formal degrees, especially women, skills such as solar engineering.
Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan
A people's organisation in Rajasthan which, with Aruna Roy and others, led the fight for the Right to Information law through public hearings.
photo_note: Village music, Abanindranath Tagore

h: CAG reports: beyond scams, a mirror of democracy's health
dek: In The Wire, Himanshu Upadhyaya writes that the value of audit is not only in catching scams, and that since 2014, delays in CAG reports and an opaque appointment process have been weakening the institution.
body: The sixth National Audit Day was marked on 16 November. On this occasion Himanshu Upadhyaya describes how he moved from the environmental movement to studying government audit, and why the Comptroller and Auditor General, the CAG, matters for the health of democracy.

In 2002, while combing newspapers for an environmental group, he came across a report that the Sardar Sarovar Narmada Nigam was raising loans from the market. Following this thread he reached the 1993 bonds and then a CAG report on Gujarat's public sector undertakings. The question arose whether audited bodies actually act on the recommendations. From 2003 he began a monthly column on CAG findings and came to see that the aim of audit is far bigger than catching fraud.

The writer raises serious questions about the CAG's independence. At present the Cabinet Secretary sends a panel of names to the Prime Minister, and the Prime Minister recommends one to the President, with no guarantee of fairness for citizens. Three public interest petitions on this are pending in the Supreme Court. He cites former CAG T.N. Chaturvedi, who later joined a party and went to the Rajya Sabha, and says a person who has held this post should not take such positions.

His second argument is about delay. According to the writer, the time taken to finalise audit reports has grown since 2014. With researcher Abhishek Punetha he compared the terms of Vinod Rai, Shashi Kant Sharma and Rajiv Mehrishi. He wants the CAG to state on its website when a report was sent to the Governor or the President and whether it was tabled.

The 1971 law on the CAG's duties and powers has not changed since, though an amendment was discussed as early as 2008. In 2009 a retired audit officer called the department incurably ill, a place with able people but no leadership.
nazar: Ordinary people heard the CAG's name during the 2G and coal allocation years, and then it seemed to vanish from the conversation. If reports come late and stay buried in assemblies, the biggest tool for demanding an account of public money becomes useless. The writer's demand to make public the dates when reports are sent and tabled is small, but it is a direct step towards accountability.
sawal: If a report never even reaches the assembly, who will answer for it?
ref: Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)
A body set up under Article 148 of the Constitution that audits the accounts of the Union and state governments and public sector undertakings and reports to Parliament and the assemblies.
photo_note: A manuscript page written in Devanagari

h: Hasina's return: justice belongs to Dhaka, but the test is a fair trial
dek: Bakhtawar Raza believes Sheikh Hasina should be tried in Bangladesh's own courts, but in a way that neither Delhi nor the world can point a finger at.
body: Amid reports of Sheikh Hasina's return to Bangladesh, six British MPs have written to Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. They want Britain to seek a guarantee from Dhaka that Hasina will not face execution, enforced disappearance, torture or political violence, that she gets a lawyer of her choice, and that there is independent monitoring of the judicial process.

The background is that in 2025 Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in her absence. Amnesty International called that trial hasty and unfair, because the lawyer appointed by the court got no time to prepare and could not even cross-examine witnesses.

In The Friday Times the writer's argument cuts both ways. On one hand, he says foreign MPs can raise human rights, but they cannot decide how Bangladesh's courts run, because the Bangladeshis who changed the government in 2024 will set the direction of their own change. On the other hand, in his view Hasina should get no exemption, but she must get an independent lawyer, protection from torture and the full right of appeal. By his reckoning, only a transparent trial will strengthen Dhaka's case.

The real key lies with India, where Hasina has lived since August 2024. Dhaka wants speedy extradition, Delhi speaks of legal process. The writer points out that the extradition treaty lets India refuse requests with a political motive, so Bangladesh's trial must pass every scrutiny.

His conclusion is that Hasina's return could remove a big cause of tension between the two countries, but ties will be normal only when there is mutual respect for sovereignty, reliable border and trade policy, and restraint in domestic politics on both sides.
nazar: This debate stands at India's door. Handing Hasina over or keeping her, either decision will shape India's image in Bangladesh. In our view Delhi's test should not be old friendship with a leader, but whether a trial carrying a death sentence guarantees a fair hearing. That is how democracy's credibility in the neighbourhood will be built.
sawal: How lasting is a sentence from a trial where the lawyer could not cross-examine?
ref: International Crimes Tribunal (Bangladesh)
A domestic Bangladeshi court set up for the war crimes of 1971, not international despite its name. After the 2024 movement it heard cases from the Hasina government's years.
India-Bangladesh extradition treaty
A treaty signed in 2013 under which the two countries hand over accused persons to each other. It leaves room for refusal in cases of offences of a political nature.
photo_note: Boats of the Nawab of Murshidabad on the Ganga

h: Africa will be built by its own markets, not Washington's favours
dek: On the decision to drop South Africa and Rwanda from a US trade concession, Hakeem Najimdeen says Africa's way forward runs through trade within the continent.
body: In September Trump extended AGOA, the US law giving trade concessions to Africa, until the end of 2028. Then on 2 November his government announced that from 1 January 2027 South Africa and Rwanda would be outside its scope. According to Nigerian analyst Hakeem Najimdeen, this is the basic weakness of the arrangement: a benefit granted by one side can be taken away by that same side at any time.

AGOA was created in 2000 and lets thousands of goods from 33 countries enter the US duty free. It is estimated to support more than three lakh direct and 13 lakh indirect jobs. But its impact is shrinking: duty-free imports fell from 7.9 billion dollars in 2024 to 5 billion dollars in 2025, and the gains stayed mostly with South Africa.

The writer says the criteria on paper are human rights and labour standards, but the decisions are driven by geopolitics. In South Africa's case, its closeness to China and Russia and Trump's 'white genocide' claims; in Rwanda's case, alleged help to the M23 rebels in eastern Congo, which clashes with US interest in the minerals there. When Ethiopia was dropped in 2022, thousands of textile workers lost their jobs.

As an alternative he looks to the African Continental Free Trade Area, which aims to build a common market of 1.3 billion people. Right now trade among African countries is only 15-18 per cent of Africa's total trade. Steps such as payments in African currencies and digital customs have already been taken.

According to the writer, the work ahead is costly but necessary: removing tariff and non-tariff barriers, building cross-border roads, railways and power grids, and instead of selling raw materials, setting up production chains that grow in one country, manufacture in another and sell within the continent.
nazar: This lesson applies to South Asia too, where trade among neighbours is even lower than in Africa and countries are taking the blows of US tariffs. In our view, when big powers start handing out trade as reward and punishment, a reliable market among neighbours is the surest insurance for workers' jobs.
sawal: Whose foreign policy took the jobs of Ethiopia's textile workers?
ref: AGOA
The African Growth and Opportunity Act, a US law of 2000 that lets goods from African countries enter America duty free. The US alone decides which countries stay in it.
African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA)
An agreement signed in Kigali in 2018, under which trading began in 2021. The goal is to gradually remove tariffs on 90 per cent of goods.
photo_note: Ox cart crossing a river, Natal

h: In the race for chips, the Aeta people's ancestral land is at stake
dek: Nadhira Muhammad Qasim says the US-led 'Pax Silica' alliance is bringing back an old kind of domination to the Philippines in the name of investment.
body: On 15 November, two days before Donald Trump arrived in Manila for the ASEAN summit, police arrested more than 200 protesters. They were opposing 'Pax Silica', the US-led alliance that wants to cut China's lead in supply chains for semiconductors, critical minerals and AI. The Philippines joined it in April 2026.

Under it, an industrial hub of about 1,618 hectares is proposed in New Clark City in Tarlac province. The government promises more than 1,30,000 jobs and up to 70 billion dollars in investment, though it will take decades to complete. The writer says local people will pay the price: about 200 people of the Aeta Hunghe community of Sapang Kawayan could lose their homes, farms, springs and burial grounds. Their claim to ancestral land has been stuck since 1994.

Water is the second question. The government agency BCDA estimates the hub will need 6.5 to 9 crore litres of water a day, while the weather agency confirmed on 4 November a very strong El Nino that could last into the first half of 2027.

The writer argues that semiconductors also go into weapons, so the project could also open the way for US military expansion. An existing defence agreement already gives the US military access to Philippine bases. In a speech on 17 November, Trump praised the growing defence cooperation.

The protests are spreading. On 13 November students of several major universities walked out of classes, there were protests in Marawi and Tawi-Tawi in Mindanao, and according to organisers there was solidarity in 23 cities in 14 countries. The writer asks the Marcos government to hear affected communities, and asks ASEAN to favour agreement among its members over the big powers.
nazar: The race for chips and AI has now reached land, water and indigenous areas, and India too is in the race to become a semiconductor hub. In our view, with every promise of 'strategic investment' we must ask whose water will go and whose home. The arrests in Manila show that even asking this is no longer easy.
sawal: Will the Aeta people's 1994 claim be heard before the factory is built?
ref: Pax Silica
A US-led alliance that wants to separate supply chains for semiconductors, critical minerals and AI infrastructure from China and make them secure. The Philippines joined it in April 2026.
Aeta
One of the oldest indigenous communities of Luzon island in the Philippines. Their traditional land claims have waited decades for government recognition.
photo_note: Women working in a paddy field

h: 787 Form 7s in Mustafabad: plea to Supreme Court for a probe
dek: Petitioners in the Delhi SIR case allege that fake objections were filed in the names of booth agents to get Muslim voters' names struck off.
body: Anjali Bhardwaj and Amrita Johri have filed a fresh application in the public interest petition pending in the Supreme Court on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter list under way in Delhi. They allege that Form 7, used to delete names, is being used to remove voters of particular communities from the list in bulk.

The application cites the Mustafabad assembly constituency, where 787 Form 7s seeking deletion of Muslim voters' names were allegedly filed in the names of 20 BJP booth level agents. According to a report in The Hindu, at least 16 of these agents said they neither filed nor authorised any such application. One agent said his details were used to try to delete the names of his own Muslim neighbours, with whom he gets along well.

The petitioners have asked that the Election Commission audit the Form 7s filed across Delhi, that FIRs be registered wherever forgery and identity theft appear, and that action be taken under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950 against those who made false declarations. All objections should be made public, and an objecting agent should clearly state his standing.

According to the application, 47,56,722 voters in Delhi were put in the 'absent, shifted, dead or duplicate' category, of whom 33,12,909 got 'no mapping' and 'logical discrepancy' notices. At the hearing on 28 October the court had already asked why voters already on the rolls were being told to fill Form 6, which is meant for new voters.
nazar: If an application to delete neighbours' votes can be filed in someone's name without their knowledge, the flaw is not just in the paperwork but in the whole process. Being struck off the list quietly shuts a citizen out of democracy, and the burden again falls on those who must prove their existence every time.
sawal: If the agent did not file the application, who filed it in his name?
ref: Form 7

An application to delete a name from the voter list or object to it.
Any voter or a party's booth agent can fill it.
Booth level agent (BLA)

Representatives appointed by political parties who watch over the list work at each booth.
Different from the government's booth level officer (BLO).
photo_note: Representative image: voting queue near the Jama Masjid, Delhi, 1952

h: Wrote about the chief minister in Ujjain, then came FIRs and exile from the city
dek: A Newslaundry investigation shows that within weeks of Mohan Yadav becoming chief minister, cases rained down on journalists who had criticised him.
body: Mohan Yadav became chief minister of Madhya Pradesh in December 2023. According to the report, within a few weeks the Ujjain journalists who had questioned him were caught up in police cases. Most FIRs allege extortion, the complaints were filed by different people, and no charge has yet been proved in court.

Abhay Tirwar, who runs a YouTube channel, had questioned the legality of a hospital run by a company whose directors include members of the chief minister's family. On the night of 3 January 2024, three FIRs were filed against him at three police stations within about three hours. When his daughter asked the police to check call records and CCTV, she herself got notices, and then parts of the family's houses were demolished. The family moved to Uttarakhand.

Rekha Goswami, editor of a weekly who wrote on the same hospital, was arrested and did not return after getting bail. Rajeev Bhadoria, who had complained to the Lokayukta (anti-corruption ombudsman), was booked the very day after Yadav became chief minister, and was later externed from Ujjain and seven neighbouring districts for a year. Jai Kaushal, who asked questions at a press conference, and Tirwar's colleague Shakeel Khan have served jail time and left journalism.
The complainants said the allegations were true or pointed to the police. The former SP declined to comment, saying the matter is in court, and there was no response from the chief minister.
nazar: Different complaints, the same timing, and the targets are the same people who were asking questions: this pattern is no longer confined to one city. Small-town journalists have neither a big institution behind them nor an army of lawyers, so silencing them needs no conviction; the case alone is enough.
sawal: Why three cases against one journalist at three police stations in the middle of the night?
ref: Zila badar (externment)

An order, in the name of law and order, for a person to stay out of a district for a set period.
In Madhya Pradesh it is issued under the state security law.
photo_note: Wrecking of a printing press, 1833

h: He showed dead fish in the Yamuna, and he was the one arrested
dek: BSP worker Surendra Singh Azad faces a case for spreading rumours, but the question of who killed the fish is still open.
body: Surendra Singh Azad, a 33-year-old BSP worker from north Delhi, has lived on the banks of the Yamuna for more than 30 years and has contested the assembly election from Timarpur. On 11 November he posted an Instagram video of dead fish floating in the river and blamed the Delhi government. The video also spread widely through Aam Aadmi Party people and the matter turned political.

The BJP's Delhi government alleged that fish were put in the river to defame the government before Chhath. An FIR was filed against unknown persons on a letter from the Irrigation and Flood Control Department, with sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita on public mischief and breach of peace. On 14 November Azad was detained in the middle of Chhath celebrations and got bail the same day. He says the police did not even tell him why he was being arrested.

Azad flatly denies putting fish in the river. He says industrial waste coming from the Najafgarh drain and a drain near Palla kills fish again and again. A local reporter in Wazirabad says this happens two or three times a year, and a fisherman at Ram Ghat pointed to dirty water from leather factories, which has turned the water black.
Newslaundry sent questions to the Pollution Control Committee and the department but got no reply.
nazar: Dead fish are proof of a sick river, but the government investigated the man who made the video instead of the drain. Calling a question about pollution a rumour and filing a case is also an injustice to a river that lakhs of people depend on for water, livelihood and faith.
sawal: Should the Najafgarh drain have been investigated first, or the video?
ref: Najafgarh drain

Delhi's biggest drain, which comes in from Haryana and falls into the Yamuna near Wazirabad.
A large part of the Yamuna's filth comes from it.
BNS Section 353

A section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita on statements likely to cause fear or public mischief.
It replaces Section 505 of the old IPC.
photo_note: Representative image: the Yamuna in Delhi, 2005

h: Ragpicker tied up and set on fire in Bengaluru
dek: Mohammed, 45, who sleeps by the roadside, has 60-70 per cent burns, and the attackers have not yet been traced.
body: In the early hours of Wednesday in Veerabhadranagar, south Bengaluru, a 45-year-old ragpicker was allegedly tied hand and foot with ropes, doused with petrol and set on fire. At about six in the morning local people found him badly burnt on the road and called the police on 112.

Police have identified him as Mohammed alias Syed H. A patrol team called an ambulance and took him to Victoria Hospital, where his condition is critical. According to the police, 60 to 70 per cent of his body is burnt.

Mohammed makes a living picking scrap. He has no proper roof, no mobile phone and no identity card. He has lived in the Padarayanapura area for years and spends his nights sleeping by the roadside. Having no papers and no address also means there is no one easily found to look after him or search for him.

Girinagar police have inspected the spot and a case is being registered. The report says nothing about who the attackers were or why they attacked, and names no suspect. No statement has yet come from the hospital, his family or fellow workers.
nazar: The people who sort a city's waste are not even counted by the city: no address, no papers, no phone. When such a man is attacked so brutally, the police investigation will also show how much the life of homeless, nameless people is worth in this city.
sawal: Who will fight for justice for a man with no identity card?
ref: Ragpickers

Unorganised workers in cities who sort dry waste and sell it.
Most work without any social security or identity papers.
photo_note: Representative image: work on a garbage heap, Mumbai

h: Israel launches new ground operation in central Gaza despite ceasefire
dek: Tanks rolled in near Nuseirat camp, families fled, and hospitals say three Palestinians were killed on the first day.
body: For the first time since the October 2025 ceasefire, Israel has launched a new ground operation in central Gaza. Hospital officials said three Palestinians were killed in it on Wednesday. Al Jazeera correspondents reported Israeli tanks moving east of Nuseirat refugee camp and north of Bureij camp near Salah al-Din Road, with drones firing from above and shelling going on.

An air strike on the town of al-Mughraqa, north of Nuseirat, killed one person and wounded several. After evacuation orders, families fled their homes in the northern part of the camp. Before the operation was announced, two more people were killed in two drone strikes in Gaza City and Deir al-Balah. Gaza's health ministry said seven deaths were recorded in the past 24 hours.

The Israeli army says the operation is to remove a threat to its soldiers posted near the 'Yellow Line', but did not say what the threat was. Hamas called it an open violation of the ceasefire and alleged that forcing people from their homes through threats and bombing is a war crime meant to cram the population into a narrow strip. Hamas held Israel and the United States responsible.
nazar: If the ceasefire holds on paper while tanks roll on the ground, all it means for the people of Gaza is that fewer deaths are counted. The silence of countries, India among them, that have hailed this ceasefire as a diplomatic success also becomes part of this operation.
sawal: What was the threat at the Yellow Line, and why did Israel not say?
ref: Yellow Line

A line drawn in the October 2025 ceasefire, behind which part of Gaza is under Israeli occupation.
There have been repeated attacks around it.
Nuseirat camp

A refugee camp in central Gaza, set up for Palestinians driven out in 1948.
It has been targeted many times in the war.
photo_note: Representative image: children on the rubble of their ruined home in Nuseirat camp (old photo)

h: Protests hurt business, so traders take the opposition to the Supreme Court
dek: The court sent notices to the parties and student group that protested against the Chief Election Commissioner, and an objection was also raised to Ramlila Maidan.
body: On Wednesday the Supreme Court issued notice to the Cockroach Janta Party, the Congress, the Aam Aadmi Party and the student group AISA on a petition by Delhi traders. The Kirana Committee Delhi and the Delhi Iron and Hardware Merchants Association say their business suffered from these groups' protests against the Chief Election Commissioner in the capital last month.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana had earlier asked the petitioners to make the organisers of the protests parties too. When the amended petition came in, the court sent notice to the new parties.

Senior advocate Mukul Rohatgi, for the traders, argued that the protests at Jantar Mantar brought business in central Delhi to a halt. He also objected to Ramlila Maidan being fixed as a protest site, saying the ground is in the heart of the city and surrounded by wholesale markets, so sit-ins should not be allowed there.

The bench said this petition will be heard along with the cases challenging restrictions imposed by officials after the protests. These cases may be listed on 27 November. Contempt petitions filed against the police and other officials will be heard on a separate day.
nazar: Places for protest in the capital are already down to a handful. If every protest begins to be weighed on the scale of lost business, the right to dissent will slowly be pushed out of the city. It is for the court to strike the balance between the market's convenience and citizens' voices.
sawal: If even Ramlila Maidan is gone, where will Delhi protest?
ref: Jantar Mantar

The place in Delhi that has long been set aside for sit-ins and protests.
In 2018 the Supreme Court lifted the total ban on protests there.
photo_note: May Day procession

h: Hundreds gather in Imphal for four civilians killed in ambush
dek: At a meeting in Mao Market, families said they will not take the bodies until they get justice, and the government has invited the groups for talks.
ask: Protection for civilians and justice for the killings
body: Hundreds of people from several indigenous communities of Manipur gathered at Mao Market in Imphal on Wednesday. The meeting was called by the Native People's Committee Manipur (NPCM) together with indigenous civil society groups. The demand was peace, security and justice.

The meeting followed the 13 November attack, when four civilians were killed in an ambush near New Haven on the Imphal-Ukhrul highway. Suspected Kuki militants are accused. The dead were a mother and son, Kapangkhui and Haolaila, of Shangshak Khullen village, and a brother and sister, Tikikas Ngalung and Tanmila Keishing, of Tashar village.

Amana Thaimai, co-convenor of the Naga Humanitarian Aid Committee Manipur, said this was the fourth attack at the same spot. Waomichon, the wife of the slain Kapangkhui, who is expecting her second child, thanked the community and demanded protection for civilians.

The new turn is that the government has invited the groups for talks. According to Thaimai, they are ready to talk, but the next step will be decided after consulting the victims' families and communities. The four bodies are in the JNIMS morgue, and the families have refused to take them until they get justice.
nazar: A fourth attack on the same road shows that the safety of people travelling on the highway is still incomplete. The decision not to take the bodies is less a sign of anger than of broken trust. The offer of talks will mean something only if it comes with a firm promise of an inquiry and of security.
sawal: How did a fourth attack happen on the same road near New Haven?
ref: JNIMS
Jawaharlal Nehru Institute of Medical Sciences, a large government hospital in Imphal. In cases of violence, bodies are often kept in its morgue.

h: Why an investment summit during a drought, 400 citizens ask Revanth Reddy
dek: With drought declared in 365 mandals, an open letter has asked for December's global summit to be put off.
ask: Postpone the summit, put the resources into drought relief
body: About 400 citizens, environmentalists, scientists, academics and people's organisations from Telangana and across the country have written an open letter to Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy, asking him to cancel or postpone the Invest Telangana Global Summit 2026, due to be held at Bharat Future City from 7 to 9 December. The letter was released on 17 November.

According to the letter, because of El Nino the state declared drought in 365 mandals (administrative blocks) across 31 districts through a government order of 24 October. Some parts of Hyderabad get a few litres of water every three or four days, schools and colleges are on holiday, and many hostels have sent children home.

The signatories argue that the lavish arrangements for an event with about 4,000 guests will burden water, power and the administration. According to a government press release, an officer will be attached to every delegate, which they see as pulling staff away from drought relief. They also recall the Chief Minister's statement of 15 October comparing El Nino to Covid.

The demand is that money, officers and staff go into drought relief and that the summit be put off until the drought order is lifted. The signatories include Prof. Shantha Sinha, Prof. D Narasimha Reddy, Lalita Ramdas, Dr. Sagari Ramdas, E A S Sarma and Prafulla Samantara. The government's response is not recorded in the report.
nazar: In a state where children are leaving hostels because of water shortage, the question of priorities is fair. Investment matters, but putting officers on hospitality duty in the middle of a drought sends the wrong message.
sawal: With 365 mandals in drought, why an officer for every guest?
ref: El Nino
The unusual warming of Pacific Ocean waters, which shows up in India as a weak monsoon and drought.

h: Mizoram journalists seek fair accreditation and advertising policy
dek: On National Press Day in Aizawl, the journalists' association said accreditation should come from clear rules, not political favour.
ask: Fair advertising policy, transparent accreditation and a media centre
body: At a National Press Day event in Aizawl on Monday, Mizoram Journalists' Association (MJA) president Vanlalrema Vantawl placed three demands before the government: a fair policy on government advertisements, transparent accreditation of journalists, and a separate media centre.

Vantawl said accreditation should be free of political considerations. He referred to earlier allegations that the government had been adding names at will. The association has written to the Directorate of Information and Public Relations asking that advertisements stop for newspapers that do not publish regularly and that working outlets get support. The demand for land for a media centre has been pending for about ten years, and the present press club is small.

The association has also cleaned its own house. About 30 members, or nearly 15 percent, were removed because they no longer work as journalists. A review of the journalists' welfare scheme, unchanged for about ten years, is almost complete.

For the government, Chief Minister Lalduhoma spoke of accurate and fair reporting. Information Minister B Lalchhanzova said welfare schemes and advertisement rates have been raised, and according to the department's secretary, a draft of a new advertising policy for print and electronic media is being prepared.
nazar: In small states, newspapers often depend on government advertising, so the policy on advertisements and accreditation ties directly to press freedom. Only if the rules are clear and public will journalists feel free to question the government.
sawal: Why have Aizawl's journalists been asking for land for ten years?
ref: National Press Day
Observed on 16 November. On this day in 1966 the Press Council of India began work.

h: On Majra villagers' complaint, NGT seeks reply from waste plant
dek: Villagers allege that leakage from a solid waste plant has poisoned wells, hand pumps and drinking water.
ask: Action against the waste plant poisoning the water
body: On a complaint from the people of Majra village in Nalagarh tehsil of Himachal Pradesh's Solan district, the principal bench of the National Green Tribunal (NGT) on 16 November asked the plant of Shivalik Solid Waste Management Limited for details of its compliance with environmental rules.

The villagers allege that leachate and waste from the plant have seeped into the groundwater. According to them, hand pumps, wells and drinking water have been contaminated, the village is filled with stench and smoke, and people's health is getting worse.

The tribunal had set up a joint committee on 16 September 2026, which submitted its report on 14 November, but the report is not yet on record. The company running the plant has now been asked how it manages leachate and the disposal of hazardous waste. The state pollution control board has also been asked to explain compliance and to report on other such plants, with a reference to a 2022 High Court order.
The next hearing is on 11 January 2027. The company's side is not recorded in the report.
nazar: In villages of industrial belts, waste plants often become neighbours without anyone asking. The report is in; any delay now means villagers drink the same water for a few more months. The tribunal should also think about interim relief.
sawal: What does the 14 November report say about Majra's water?
ref: TSDF
Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facility: a site for treating, storing and disposing of hazardous industrial waste, governed by strict rules.

h: Searches in Kulgam for a seventh day, leaders call it collective punishment
dek: House searches and curbs on movement around Akhran and the Laroo bypass have brought daily life to a halt.
ask: End collective punishment in the name of searches
body: In parts of south Kashmir's Kulgam district, movement remained restricted for the seventh day running on Tuesday, 17 November. Armed personnel are searching house to house and people are being frisked again and again. Roads in and out are sealed and orchards are being searched too.

The operation began after the 11 November attack on a CRPF post at Akhran, Nowpora, in which three personnel were injured. On 16 November a body was found at the encounter site on the Laroo bypass and identified as Umar Nisar Dar, a baker from Kulgam. He was not a listed militant. Agencies suspect he was involved in the attack, while his family had filed a missing person report.

Kulgam MLA Mohammad Yousuf Tarigami said making people stand outside their homes on freezing nights is no solution. Mehbooba Mufti said Akhran has been turned into a garrison and that collective punishment only deepens alienation. Mirwaiz Umar Farooq called the treatment of the elderly, women and children inhuman.
No government statement on the criticism is recorded in the report.
nazar: The attack must be investigated, but keeping a whole area in near captivity for a week weighs heavily on ordinary people's rights. Trust will not return without a clear answer on the death of a baker and his family's missing person report.
sawal: How did a missing bakery worker end up at an encounter site?
ref: Cordon and search operation
An operation in which security forces surround an area, restrict movement in and out, and search house to house.

h: Idols immersed on Karimnagar farmers' land, High Court pulls up officials
dek: On a contempt petition, the Collector assured the court that the 33 guntas of land will be returned to the farmers in their original state.
ask: Return the land or pay compensation under the law
body: The Telangana High Court sharply reprimanded the Karimnagar district administration on Tuesday. Justice C V Bhaskar Reddy was hearing the farmers' contempt petition, which said officials had not followed the court's earlier directions.

The case concerns 33 guntas of the farmers' private patta (titled) land, which was used for immersing Bathukamma and Ganesh idols. According to the farmers' lawyer, the land was occupied for three years, gravel was laid, street lights were put up, and in return one acre of other land was promised but never given. Then the administration said it did not need the land at all.

The court asked how the land could be called unnecessary when neither alternative land was given nor was it acquired under the law with compensation paid. Collector Chitra Mishra, appearing online, said the land is now within the municipal corporation, falls in a lake's full tank level area and was not being farmed.

In the end the Collector assured the court that the land will be returned in its original state and that orders will also bar temporary public use in future. The court recorded this and reserved its final order.
nazar: Using private land for three years without compensation and then calling it 'unnecessary' shows how easily the state machinery treats a small farmer's land as its own. The court has shown the way; now to see when the land is actually returned.
sawal: Why was the promise of one acre to Karimnagar's farmers forgotten?
ref: Gunta
A unit of land measurement in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. 40 guntas make one acre.

h: Ladakh's glacier died, and now the mosquitoes have come
dek: In Leh district, a warming climate, weak health infrastructure and unplanned tourism have opened a path for malaria and dengue that never existed here before.
body: The village of Sakti in Leh district sits at about 3,900 metres. Here 65-year-old Gelek Gyurmet is the keeper of the village's artificial glacier. One June morning he checks the pipes, watches the stream of meltwater and finds that this store of ice is shrinking before its time. Vidya Krishnan's report tells us that the village's real glacier vanished five years ago, and where there was once ice there is now a grassy meadow.

About four hundred families live in Sakti, most of them from the Boto community, Ladakh's largest Scheduled Tribe, which has raised yaks, goats and sheep for generations. In place of the glacier the villagers have built a 'khangri', a structure that stores winter snow, whose water is slowly released to the fields in summer. The elders say that for two or three decades there has been neither that kind of snowfall nor that kind of winter.

Along with this heat has come a new visitor: the mosquito. According to the report, Ladakh recorded its first two dengue cases in 2022, and with that no state or union territory in the country remained untouched by it. There were two malaria cases in 2024 and three in 2025. Officials treat these as cases brought in by tourists from outside, but there are other signs too: ceiling fans are being installed in homes for the first time, mosquito repellents are selling in the market, and mosquitoes have started to appear in the lower villages around Leh.

Retired doctor Tsering Norboo, a Padma Shri awardee, says unplanned construction, water shortage and rising heat are together raising the risk. Dr. Yogesh Jain of Jan Swasthya Sahyog believes that even imported cases can infect local mosquitoes and let the disease spread here, so mosquito surveys and monitoring are needed right now.

The trouble is that there is no monitoring system at all. According to the report, Ladakh's government labs can do basic tests, but for deeper study of how an infection is spreading, samples have to be sent to Delhi or Chandigarh, and there is not a single accredited lab to test drinking water quality. Leh's college and university have no public health department. Leh's Chief Medical Officer did not answer the writer's questions.
nazar: Ladakh's story shows that the climate crisis is not only about melting ice but also about health. A government that talks of a 2030 target to end malaria has not managed to set up even one lab in the very region where the disease is arriving for the first time. Villages like Sakti, which have the least hand in this warming, are the first to pay its price.
sawal: Where there is no lab to test water, who will catch dengue?
ref: Khangri (artificial glacier)

A structure made by collecting winter snow on slopes.
In summer its meltwater is used to irrigate the fields.
Aedes mosquito

The mosquitoes that spread dengue, chikungunya and Zika.
With rising heat they are spreading to higher and drier areas.
photo_note: Snowy Himalayan mountains, representative image

h: Mothers warned of danger, courts handed the children to fathers
dek: Through two American mothers, this Al Jazeera Fault Lines film asks why warnings of domestic violence go unheard even after they reach family court.
body: This film, 'Fatal Custody', from Al Jazeera English's investigative series Fault Lines, goes into the part of America's family courts where, after a divorce, it is decided how much time children will spend with whom. The film, about thirty-two minutes long, moves through the stories of two mothers, Hope Hooton and Kelly Elliott.

Both mothers feared their children were not safe with their fathers. Hope sought protection from the court when her husband threatened suicide, and he later also went through a serious mental health crisis. Kelly had formally documented years of domestic violence and abuse.

Even so, in both cases the fathers kept getting unsupervised time with the children. According to the film, it was during this time that those fathers killed their children. The very danger the mothers had been pointing to came true, and the system could not stop it.

Through these two stories the film examines how evidence of danger gets ignored, dismissed, or sometimes never reaches family court at all. The question is not about one judge or one case, but about the whole structure in which these decisions are made.

Fault Lines also lays out the debate over the growing push in America for equal custody, that is, giving both parents equal rights and time with the children. According to the film, one major gap is that violence against a child's mother or father is not seen as a danger to the child.

Finally, the film turns to the changes that activists working on this issue are demanding. They say that if courts weigh a history of domestic violence seriously, other families can be spared such harm. The film announces no verdict, but leaves viewers with the question of who is accountable when a warning has already been given.
nazar: This story is from America, but its question is for courts in every country. Domestic violence is often treated as a private quarrel between husband and wife and kept apart from the child's safety, when in one home the two are bound together. When a woman's complaint is brushed aside as 'revenge', children often pay the price.

In India too, domestic violence allegations in divorce and custody cases hang fire for a long time. The film reminds us that the principle of equality in law becomes justice only when it gives equal weight to evidence of danger as well.
sawal: Why do courts not give a mother's warning the weight of a danger to the child?
ref: Fault Lines
Al Jazeera English's investigative documentary series. It takes long looks at issues of power, justice and rights in America and around the world.
Family court
A court for family matters, which hears disputes such as divorce, maintenance and child custody. The child's interest is taken as its main yardstick.
Equal custody
The principle that after a divorce children spend roughly equal time with both parents. Critics say it can be dangerous in cases involving violence.
photo_note: A still from the film

h: Priyadarshi, gone at forty-three, and the books he did not write
dek: Krishna Samiddh's memoir-essay remembers the young poet and lawyer Priyadarshi 'Matrisharan' not with sentiment but with an honest reading.
body: Priyadarshi 'Matrisharan' was born in 1983 and died this year at 43. He leaves behind his parents, his wife Shikha and two children. He was a lawyer by profession, and according to the writer, his experience in court shaped both his sense of justice and his prose. When 'Samayik Vimarsh', edited by Madan Kashyap, published his poems, he came to be seen as a promising new poet.

Krishna Samiddh, a poet, critic and theatre and film director, also sets out the family background. His grandfather Rajendra Prasad Singh was a minister in Bihar, and Priyadarshi considered him his first teacher of language. His great-grandfather Banarsi Prasad Singh was a freedom fighter, a member of the Constituent Assembly and was elected to the Lok Sabha three times.

According to the writer, by November 2025 Priyadarshi had prepared a collection of 82 poems, 'Ek Vakil ki Likha-Padhi' (A Lawyer's Writings), but held back its publication to rework it. His English novel 'In the Face of Love' was completed after about ten years, while his Hindi novel 'Prathamva' remained unfinished. In an extract from it, a poor boy's very name is turned into a slur, and child labour and class contempt come to the surface.

The essay says that when a minority friend was threatened with a police case, Priyadarshi stood by him openly and had to face a silent boycott for it. Ten days before his death, back from hospital, he was learning Urdu poetry from a friend.

Samiddh divides his poems into three styles: aphoristic, dramatic and reflective-narrative. Poems like 'Mazdoor' (Labourer) ask whether literature can portray suffering justly. Seven unpublished poems and the extract from the novel are printed with the essay.
nazar: In Hindi, when a young writer dies, tributes often last two days and then there is silence. Samiddh's plea is the reverse: honouring a dead writer means reading him seriously. In Deshkaal's view this plea matters all the more because Priyadarshi's greatest wealth was what he was yet to write.
sawal: If the unfinished 'Prathamva' is published, how will Hindi read it?
ref: Samayik Vimarsh
A Hindi magazine edited by Madan Kashyap, in which Priyadarshi's poems were published.
Memoir criticism
Writing in which memories of a writer and criticism of their work run side by side.
photo_note: Villagers of Raniya, around 1816

h: Money, education, and still a woman loses out in the paperwork
dek: Dr. Nidhi Agrawal's essay asks how a woman can be called empowered if she cannot understand her own property, documents and government offices.
body: Nidhi Agrawal, a doctor by profession, argues that a woman's fight is often not with one man but with the whole system: family, society and the bureaucracy, which mostly lean towards men. Until a woman has control over her property, legal papers and dealings with government offices, talk of empowerment is hollow.

She begins with the case of Shakereh Khaleeli, brought back into discussion by the Prime Video documentary series 'Dancing on the Grave'. Wealthy and educated, Shakereh disappeared in 1991, and in 1994 her remains were found in a large box in the courtyard of her Bengaluru home. Her second husband, Murali Manohar Mishra alias Shraddhananda, was convicted. According to the writer, he had obtained a power of attorney and for years ran business with her forged signatures, while distance from her family had left Shakereh isolated.
The writer asks whether wealth is the same as capability. She says Indian upbringing teaches daughters good manners but does not give them the tools to protect their rights and property.

There are more examples: a gynaecologist friend who performs difficult operations with ease but panics at a government letter and depends on a violent husband; Chanda, whose husband transferred her property to his brother's name; a woman whose land, bought with a lifetime's savings, had been sold several times through forged registrations. Citing Ramanika Gupta's autobiography 'Aaphudri' (Headstrong), she shows that even powerful women often lean on some male protector.

As remedies she calls for compulsory financial and legal education in schools, teaching boys about shared property and non-violent relationships, and making registration, mutation (dakhil-kharij) and inheritance procedures transparent.
nazar: Official empowerment figures count bank accounts and schemes; this essay looks at the woman standing at the tehsil (sub-district office) window. In Deshkaal's view this is the real yardstick: can she read, understand and protect her own papers without some powerful man.
sawal: Does the registry office take a woman seriously when she comes alone?
ref: Mukhtarnama
Power of attorney: a document giving one person the right to handle property or legal matters on another's behalf.
Dakhil-kharij
The process of changing the owner's name in government land records, also called mutation.
photo_note: Portrait of a woman, Abanindranath Tagore

h: Panna's tigers are back, but whose forest is it?
dek: Sandip Naik reads Sonal's novel 'Yeh Jiska Jungle Hai' as the human story of Panna Tiger Reserve's revival, and also counts its silences.
body: Sonal's novel 'Yeh Jiska Jungle Hai' (Whose Forest This Is), subtitled 'Chakravyuh Mein Baagh' (The Tiger in the Trap), is published by Neolit Prakashan and runs to 282 pages. According to reviewer Sandip Naik, it is not just a story of tigers returning to the forest but a serious look at the changing relationship between the forest, biodiversity, people and nature.

The reviewer says Sonal is not a writer who watches from a distance. About 35 years of social work and travel through dense forests, along the Narmada and to remote villages show in the novel. She has also written poetry, diaries, reportage and a book on the making of the film 'Kalichat'.

The story centres on Panna Tiger Reserve. The review recalls that because of poaching and failed protection, tigers had vanished there by 2009. During the time of field director R S Srinivas Murthy, tigresses were brought from Kanha and Bandhavgarh, and later male tigers. According to the reviewer, the novel shows this revival not as an official achievement but as human labour full of meetings, disagreements, doubts and small victories. He also finds its blend of Hindi, local dialect and English natural.

But the reviewer's complaints are clear too. In many places the detail is more than needed and events repeat. The writer seems hesitant in criticising government schemes. Accountability, administrative lapses, local people's rights and the commercial interests of tourism needed sharper analysis, and Adivasi (indigenous) and rural voices should have had more space.
Even so, his conclusion is that the book is useful for schools, colleges and social organisations, because it links government data with emotional understanding.
nazar: Counting tigers is the easiest yardstick, so governments seek applause for it. The reviewer's plea that success should also be measured by the health of the forest and its ties with nearby communities sharpens the question in the novel's title. In Deshkaal's view, a story of the forest is incomplete without those who live in it.
sawal: Where are the nearby villages in the count of Panna's tigers?
ref: Panna Tiger Reserve
A tiger reserve in Madhya Pradesh where, after tigers had vanished by 2009, the population was rebuilt by bringing in tigers from other reserves.
Reportage
An eyewitness account of an event or place, written in a literary style.
photo_note: Studies of a resting tiger, Punjab Hills, 18th century

h: Arpita Singh: reckoning with violence through everyday life
dek: In his column, Ashok Vajpeyi remembers the painter Arpita Singh as a fearless recorder of the violence of our times.
body: In this instalment of 'Kabhi-Kabhar' (Now and Then), Ashok Vajpeyi writes on the painter Arpita Singh, who had long been ill but remained active in thought and art. She spoke little and did not claim credit for her work, yet her paintings had an unhesitating, uncompromising resolve. Vajpeyi calls her a fearless historian of the violence spread across our times.

According to the writer, many of her paintings place the tenderness and dignity of the world right beside its unbridled cruelty. Few of her contemporaries resisted and questioned modern violence so much. Her inner search reached social truth on its own, and her visual language, made of imagination, memory, unease and grace, communicated even while being complex.

Vajpeyi stresses that Arpita Singh's truth was not seen from afar but lived and seen up close. Her paintings have no heroes, only ordinary people, and a woman's slightly sideways, gently ironic gaze, which exposes distortion but does not let go of compassion. He recalls the 1987 exhibition at Bharat Bhavan in Bhopal, which Jagdish Swaminathan put together from the work of four women painters, and where many people saw her paintings together for the first time.

In the next part of the column Vajpeyi writes that dictatorship keeps trying to convince people that there is no alternative. Citing Vaclav Havel, he calls love, friendship, sympathy and tolerance the foundation of society, and reads the elections in America, Brazil and Serbia and the non-violent protests of young people in India as signs of an alternative taking shape.

The last part, drawing on a new book by Ramin Jahanbegloo, is on Iran: repression, the fatwa against Salman Rushdie and exiled writers on one side, and music, miniature painting, architecture and literature on the other. Vajpeyi's conclusion is that freedom needs beauty and beauty needs freedom.
nazar: It does not seem a coincidence that a column on an artist like Arpita Singh turns to dictatorship and alternatives. To say, in memory of a painter who saw the violence of the kitchen and the street, that beauty cannot survive without freedom is, in Deshkaal's view, the most necessary art criticism of today.
sawal: Who will take an initiative like the 1987 Bharat Bhavan exhibition today?
ref: Kabhi-Kabhar
Ashok Vajpeyi's weekly column, which began in Jansatta in 1997 and now appears in The Wire Hindi.
Bharat Bhavan
A multi-arts centre in Bhopal, opened in 1982; Jagdish Swaminathan was associated with its Roopankar museum of fine arts.
photo_note: Shakuntala writing a letter

h: A seven-kilo typewriter and a thirty-year column
dek: Sanjeev Kumar Choubey, who was Ashok Vajpeyi's assistant, recalls the world of fax, phone and typewriter behind 'Kabhi-Kabhar'.
body: Ashok Vajpeyi's column 'Kabhi-Kabhar' (Now and Then) began in 1997 as a Sunday column in Jansatta and then moved to Deshbandhu, Satyagrah, Jansandesh Times and The Wire Hindi. Sanjeev Kumar Choubey, who was Vajpeyi's assistant and the first to read this column running for nearly three decades, writes his inside memories of it.

It begins with the 2000 book 'Kabhi-Kabhar', found at his village home, whose first five copies Arun Maheshwari brought to the Shahjahan Road house in August 2000. On the writer's copy, Vajpeyi had written thanks for sending and correcting many columns.

The writer came into this work at about eighteen. In the very first week, the envelope of typed pages did not reach the Noida office, so for about a year and a half the column went by fax. Once, when the fax broke down, the column was missed, and after that he began phoning to confirm it had arrived. At Jansatta, Manglesh Dabral and Priyadarshan kept helping.

The memories hold small, lively details: phoning the painter Raza in France for Vajpeyi while he was abroad, and forgetting the time difference; a typewriter of about seven kilos that went everywhere and on which every column was typed; repairing a worn ribbon at the housing society gate during the 2020 lockdown, and Vajpeyi keeping it in 'quarantine' for two days. From 2012 he sent the column every week to Krishna Baldev Vaid and Champa Vaid in America; Vaid's last email was from April 2017.

According to the writer, after Om Thanvi retired in 2016, Jansatta's new editor seemed uneasy with the column's sharp comments, and the column left for other homes. Piyush Daiya put the clippings together into two books, which came out from Vani Prakashan in 2011.
nazar: A column changing newspapers is often a one-line item, but this memoir shows that writing which says sharp things has had to find a new home again and again. In Deshkaal's view it is also a small record of Hindi journalism's changing tolerance.
sawal: What did the exit of 'Kabhi-Kabhar' from Jansatta signal?
ref: Krishna Baldev Vaid
An experimental Hindi fiction writer ('Uska Bachpan', 'Bimal urf Jaayen to Jaayen Kahan'), who lived in America in his later years.
Syed Haider Raza
An Indian painter settled in France, famous for his 'Bindu' series; a close friend of Ashok Vajpeyi.
photo_note: The End of the Journey, Abanindranath Tagore
